sections.h2: What Are Dental Sealants & How Do They Work?
body: Dental sealants are thin, tooth-colored acrylic coatings that are painted onto the chewing surfaces of the back teeth — the molars and premolars. These teeth contain deep pits and grooves that act as natural traps for food particles and the bacteria that cause cavities.

Even thorough brushing and flossing can't always reach the bottom of these grooves, leaving them vulnerable to decay. Dental sealants effectively "seal" these grooves — filling them in and creating a smooth, flat surface that's much easier to keep clean with normal brushing.

The result? A highly effective physical barrier that protects the tooth enamel from plaque and acids, dramatically reducing the risk of cavities forming in the most decay-prone areas of the mouth. The CDC reports that school-age children without sealants have almost 3 times more cavities than those with sealants.

body: Dental sealants aren't just for kids — both children and adults can benefit from this simple, highly effective preventive treatment.

Children & Teenagers: The most important time to apply sealants is shortly after the permanent molars erupt — typically between ages 6–12. The first molars appear around age 6, and the second molars around age 12. Applying sealants as soon as these teeth emerge provides protection during the highest-risk years for cavities.

Adults at Risk for Cavities: Adults without existing fillings or decay in their back teeth can also benefit significantly from sealants. If your molars have deep, pronounced grooves — or if you have a history of frequent cavities — sealants provide an additional layer of defense on top of regular brushing, flossing, and cleanings.

Not sure if sealants are right for you or your child? Dr. Brown will assess your back teeth at your next checkup and let you know if sealants would provide a meaningful benefit. There's never any pressure — just honest, personalized guidance.

body: The entire sealant application takes only a few minutes per tooth — no drilling, no injections, no discomfort. Here's exactly what happens.

No drilling. No anaesthesia. No pain. Patients can eat and drink normally immediately after the appointment. Sealants can often be applied at the same visit as a routine cleaning — maximizing your time.
bullets: Clean the Tooth — the tooth to be sealed is thoroughly cleaned to remove any plaque or food debris. The surface is then dried with air to prepare for the bonding process.
Etch the Surface — a mild acidic gel (etching solution) is applied briefly to the chewing surface. This slightly roughens the enamel so the sealant bonds firmly and durably to the tooth.
Apply the Sealant — the tooth is rinsed and dried again, then the liquid sealant material is carefully painted onto the grooves and pits of the chewing surface, flowing into all the tiny crevices.
Cure with Light — a special curing light is held over the tooth for a few seconds to harden the sealant. That's it — no waiting, no discomfort. The tooth is sealed and protected immediately.

faqs.a: Dental sealants are thin, tooth-colored acrylic coatings that are painted onto the chewing (occlusal) surfaces of the back teeth — molars and premolars. These teeth have deep pits and grooves that are difficult to clean thoroughly with a toothbrush alone, making them the most cavity-prone teeth in the mouth. The sealant material flows into these grooves and hardens, creating a smooth, protective barrier that prevents food particles and bacteria from getting trapped and causing decay. They are invisible, tooth-colored, and provide protection for years.

faqs.q: Are dental sealants just for children?
faqs.a: Not at all. While sealants are most commonly recommended for children and teenagers — particularly after permanent molars erupt around ages 6 and 12 — adults can also benefit significantly from sealants. If you are an adult with deep molar grooves, a history of frequent cavities, or back teeth that are still free of existing fillings and decay, sealants can provide meaningful protection. Dr. Brown will assess your back teeth and let you know whether sealants would be a worthwhile investment for your specific situation.

No — applying dental sealants is completely painless. There is no drilling, no injections, and no anaesthesia required. The procedure involves cleaning the tooth, applying a brief etching solution, rinsing, and then painting on the sealant material and curing it with a light. The entire process takes only a few minutes per tooth. Most patients — including young, anxious children — have no difficulty whatsoever with the procedure.

faqs.q: How long do dental sealants last?
faqs.a: Dental sealants hold up well under the force of normal chewing and can last several years — typically 5 to 10 years or longer with proper care. They are checked at every routine dental checkup to ensure they are still intact and providing full protection. If a sealant chips, wears down, or shows signs of breakdown, it can be easily and quickly reapplied. Even partial sealant coverage continues to provide some protective benefit.

faqs.q: Are dental sealants covered by dental insurance?
faqs.a: Many dental insurance plans cover sealants for children — typically up to age 14 or 18 — because they are classified as a preventive treatment. Coverage for adults varies by plan. Our team will verify your specific benefits before your appointment and let you know exactly what is covered. Even without full insurance coverage, the out-of-pocket cost of sealants is modest — and far less than the cost of treating a cavity, filling, crown, or root canal that the sealant prevents.

faqs.q: How effective are sealants at preventing cavities?
faqs.a: Highly effective. According to the American Dental Association and the CDC, dental sealants protect against up to 80% of cavities in the back teeth during the first two years after application, and continue to protect against up to 50% of cavities for up to four years. The CDC also reports that school-age children without sealants have almost three times more cavities than those with sealants. When you consider the time, discomfort, and expense of treating cavities, sealants represent one of the most cost-effective preventive treatments in all of dentistry.

faqs.q: Can a sealant be placed over a tooth that already has a small cavity?
faqs.a: In some cases, a sealant may be placed over a very early-stage cavity in a groove or pit — effectively sealing the bacteria inside and halting further progression of the decay. However, this is only appropriate in specific clinical situations and at Dr. Brown's discretion. If decay has progressed beyond the very earliest stage, a filling or other restoration will be required first. Dr. Brown will examine your teeth carefully before recommending sealants to ensure they are appropriate and beneficial for your specific situation.
